title: ACT Reading Strategy: Read Fast, Answer Smart
summary: A complete method for the ACT Reading section: a 10-minute-per-passage time plan, active reading with a 3-word map, smart question order and trap-based elimination, with a full practice passage.

blocks.text: What the ACT Reading section looks like

The enhanced ACT Reading section gives you **36 questions in 40 minutes**. **27 of the questions are scored**: they come from **3 scored passages with 9 questions each**. The other 9 questions are not scored, but you cannot rely on spotting them, so treat every passage as if it counts. There is **no penalty for wrong answers**, so never leave a question blank.

rows: 3 passages, 9 questions each: two of about 750 words and one of about 650 words
1 literary narrative (fiction or memoir) + 2 informational passages (humanities, social science or natural science)
Each test form has either a paired-passage set (two shorter texts) or a passage with charts or graphs

blocks.text: The questions are reported in three categories. You will study each one on its own page in this course.

headers: What it asks you to do
rows: Find the main idea, locate details, follow sequence and cause–effect, make inferences
Explain word meaning in context, purpose, structure, point of view and tone
Compare two passages, use charts and tables, judge arguments and evidence

blocks.text: Typical question stems (in our own words) look like this: "The main purpose of the passage is to:", "According to the passage, …", "Based on paragraph 3, it can most reasonably be inferred that …", "As it is used in line 12, the word "x" most nearly means:", "The third paragraph mainly functions to:". Many ACT Reading stems end with a colon, so the correct choice completes the sentence.

blocks.title: الفكرة الأساسية
blocks.text: الـ Reading فيه 36 سؤال في 40 دقيقة، يعني 4 قطع كل واحدة 9 أسئلة. ادي كل قطعة حوالي 10 دقايق بس: 3 لـ 4 دقايق قراية والباقي للأسئلة. مفيش خصم على الغلط، فمتسيبش ولا سؤال فاضي.
Step 1: The time plan

36 questions in 40 minutes means four sets of 9 questions in about **10 minutes per set**. That is the whole plan. Write the target times at the top of your scrap paper (or keep them in your head) and check the clock after each passage.

rows: Passage 4 — and every answer filled in

items: **Reading: 3–4 minutes** for a 650–750-word passage. This is a fast, active read, not a slow study.
**Questions: about 6 minutes**, which is about 40 seconds per question. Some take 15 seconds, some take 70.
**If you are behind**: never "finish" a passage by spending 15 minutes on it. Guess on the slowest question, move on, and come back if you have time.
**Last two minutes**: fill in an answer for every question you have not reached. A guess can score; a blank cannot.

blocks.text: Step 2: Active reading — the 3-word map

Most students lose time because they read the passage once slowly, then read it again for every question. The fix is to read once, quickly, with a purpose: after each paragraph, write (or think) its main idea in **about three words**. This gives you a map. When a question asks about "the claim about tickets", your map tells you it is in paragraph 3, and you go straight there.

items: **Read the blurb first.** The short introduction above the passage tells you the type (literary narrative, social science, humanities, natural science) and often the topic. Ten seconds, free information.
**Read the first paragraph and the last paragraph a little more carefully.** They usually hold the main idea and the author's final position.
**In the middle paragraphs, read the first one or two sentences carefully and move faster through the examples.** You can come back to details later; you only need to know where they are.
**After each paragraph, write a 3-word label**, e.g. [2] empty time stretches, [3] uncertainty → tickets, [4] fairness → one line.
**Notice the signal words** that turn the argument: however, but, yet, critics, in fact, finally. Circle them mentally. Questions love the sentence that comes after "however".
**At the end, say the main idea in one sentence** before you look at question 1.

blocks.text: Here is what a 3-word map of the practice passage on this page could look like. Do not read it yet if you want to try the passage cold.
Step 3: Question order — answer the easy ones first
Inside a passage you can answer the 9 questions in any order. A smart order saves time:

items: **First: line- or paragraph-reference questions** ("In paragraph 3…", "As it is used in line 8…"). They tell you exactly where to look, so they are fast.
**Second: other detail questions** that name a clear key word ("tickets", "amusement parks"). Use your map to find the paragraph.

**Last: big-picture questions** (main idea, main purpose, author's overall attitude). By the time you reach them, you have answered eight questions about the passage, so you understand it better than you did after one reading.

blocks.text: On the ACT, the first question of a set is often a big-picture question. That does not mean you must answer it first. Skip it, answer the reference questions, then return to it.
Step 4: Line-reference vs big-picture questions

rows: Names a line, a paragraph or a quoted phrase
Go back. Read the sentence before, the sentence itself and the sentence after. Answer in your own words, then match.
"According to the passage" + a specific topic
Use your map to find the paragraph; scan for the key word; read around it.
"main idea", "main purpose", "overall", "the passage as a whole"
Use your one-sentence summary. The right answer must cover the WHOLE passage, not one paragraph.
The answer is not written word for word, but it must be ONE small step from the text. If you need two steps or outside knowledge, it is wrong.

blocks.title: Answer before you look
blocks.text: For every question, cover the choices and form a short answer in your own words first ("because they had something to look at"). Then uncover the choices and pick the one that matches. This protects you from attractive wrong answers that were written to sound clever.
Step 5: Elimination — find the one word that kills a choice
Three of the four choices are wrong, and each was written with a reason to be wrong. Learn the trap names; when you can name the trap, you can cross the choice out with confidence.

rows: Covers much more than the passage or the paragraph
Only one detail when the question asks about the whole
always, never, all, prove, completely, only
The first half is true, the second half is not in the text
"…but customers can no longer choose a cashier they like"
Says the opposite of the passage, often using the passage's own words
True in real life, but the passage never says it
"to give staff time to prepare the ride"
True somewhere in the passage, but not in the lines asked about
A paragraph 6 idea for a paragraph 2 question

blocks.title: الاستبعاد
blocks.text: متدورش على الإجابة اللي «شكلها حلوة». دور على الكلمة اللي بتبوظ الاختيار: always أو never أو نص جملة مش موجودة في القطعة. لو في كلمة واحدة غلط، الاختيار كله غلط. والإجابة الصح لازم تقدر تحط صباعك على الجملة اللي بتثبتها في القطعة.
Worked examples
Read this short excerpt (it is shorter than a real ACT passage, so we can focus on the method). Then study how each question is solved and why each wrong choice fails.

[1] In many neighbourhoods, a new kind of refrigerator has appeared on the pavement. Known as a community fridge, it belongs to no one in particular: anyone may leave food in it, and anyone may take food out. Supporters describe the fridges as a simple answer to two problems at once, the food that shops and households throw away and the families who cannot afford enough to eat.

[2] The idea is not without difficulties. Someone must clean the fridge, check that the food is still safe, and pay for the electricity. In several cities, fridges that began with great enthusiasm were quietly removed within a year because no volunteer group had agreed to look after them. The fridges that last, it seems, are those adopted by an existing organization, such as a mosque, a school or a local café, whose members already meet every day.

[3] What the fridges offer, then, is less a technical solution than a social one. The machine itself is ordinary; what makes it work is a group of neighbours willing to share responsibility for it.
**Worked example 1 — a paragraph-reference question**
**Question:** According to paragraph 2, community fridges are most likely to last when they are:

items: A) placed in neighbourhoods with many shops.
B) filled with food from large supermarkets.
C) looked after by an organization whose members meet regularly.
D) paid for by the city government.

blocks.text: **Answer: C.** Paragraph 2 ends: "The fridges that last … are those adopted by an existing organization … whose members already meet every day." Answer in your own words first ("when a group looks after them"), and C matches.

items: **A is wrong** — Off-topic: shops are mentioned only in paragraph 1, as a source of wasted food, not as a reason fridges last (wrong place).
**B is wrong** — Outside knowledge: the passage never says where the food comes from in the lasting fridges.
**D is wrong** — Electricity costs are mentioned as a difficulty, but the passage never says the government pays (not in the text).

blocks.text: **Worked example 2 — a big-picture question**
**Question:** The main idea of the excerpt is that community fridges:

items: A) succeed or fail mainly because of whether people take shared responsibility for them.
B) are a technical invention that has solved the problem of food waste.
C) were removed from most cities within a year of being installed.
D) should be replaced by food banks run by professional staff.

blocks.text: **Answer: A.** Paragraph 3 states the conclusion: the fridges are "less a technical solution than a social one". Paragraph 2 supports it with the volunteer problem. A covers the whole excerpt.

items: **B is wrong** — Reversed: the author says they are less a technical solution than a social one, and nothing says the problem is "solved" (too extreme).
**C is wrong** — Too extreme and too narrow: "several" fridges were removed, not "most", and that is one detail, not the main idea.
**D is wrong** — Outside the passage: food banks and professional staff are never mentioned.

blocks.text: **Worked example 3 — an inference question**
**Question:** Based on the excerpt, it can most reasonably be inferred that the fridges removed "within a year" (paragraph 2) failed mainly because:

items: A) people in those neighbourhoods did not need free food.
B) the fridges were of poor technical quality.
C) the food left in them was usually unsafe.
D) no group took on the work of maintaining them.

blocks.text: **Answer: D.** The sentence itself gives the reason: they were removed "because no volunteer group had agreed to look after them." D is a one-step inference; the passage practically states it.

items: **A is wrong** — Not supported: the passage says the fridges serve families who cannot afford food; nothing suggests those neighbourhoods lacked need.
**B is wrong** — Reversed: paragraph 3 says "the machine itself is ordinary"; the problem was people, not the machine.
**C is wrong** — Too extreme ("usually") and never stated; checking food safety is listed as a task, not as the cause of failure.

blocks.title: Classic traps
items: **Reading the whole passage slowly, then rereading for every question.** Read once, fast, with a 3-word map.
**Choosing the answer that "sounds smart" or is true in real life.** If you cannot point to the sentence that proves it, it is wrong.
**Picking a detail for a main-idea question.** The main idea must fit the first AND the last paragraph.
**Half-right choices.** Read every choice to the last word; the error is often at the end.
**Spending 15 minutes on one passage.** The fourth passage is worth exactly as much as the first. Protect your 10 minutes per set.

blocks.title: Fast strategy for test day
items: Check the clock at 30, 20 and 10 minutes left: one passage per 10 minutes.
Blurb → first paragraph → middle paragraphs fast → last paragraph → one-sentence main idea.
Reference questions first, big-picture questions last.
Answer in your own words before looking at the choices.
Eliminate by naming the trap: too broad, too extreme, half-right, reversed, outside knowledge, wrong place.
Never leave a blank: there is no penalty for wrong answers.

blocks.text: Practice

Now try a full-length passage (about 700 words, social science) with 9 questions, as on the real test. It is **untimed** so you can practise the method, but note how long it takes you: your goal on test day is about 10 minutes. Read the passage once with a 3-word map, answer the reference questions first, and save question 1 for last.

blocks.title: ACT Reading practice — Social Science passage
blocks.intro: One passage, 9 questions, untimed. Use the 3-word map, answer in your own words first, and eliminate by naming the trap. Explanations appear at the end.

questions.p:
SOCIAL SCIENCE: This passage is adapted from an essay about the psychology of waiting in line.

[1] Nobody enjoys standing in line, yet most of us spend a surprising part of our lives doing it: at the bank, at the pharmacy counter, at the gate of a stadium on match day. What people who study waiting have found, however, is that the misery of a line has less to do with the minutes on the clock than with the minutes in our heads. Two people can wait exactly the same length of time and walk away with completely different memories of the experience. For the businesses and public offices that make us wait, this gap between real time and felt time has become a practical problem worth solving.

[2] The first principle is that empty time stretches. When there is nothing to do, attention turns inward and lands on the waiting itself, and a person who checks the clock every thirty seconds will judge five minutes to be far longer than it was. A story often told in management courses describes a tall office building whose tenants kept complaining that the elevators were too slow. Engineers proposed expensive upgrades, but a manager suggested something cheaper: mirrors beside the elevator doors. The complaints largely stopped, not because the elevators moved any faster but because people now had something to look at—themselves. Whether or not every detail of the story is true, it captures an idea that later research has supported: occupied time feels shorter than unoccupied time.

[3] A second principle concerns uncertainty. A wait of unknown length is more stressful than a longer wait whose end is visible. This is why many clinics and government offices now hand out numbered tickets and display the number currently being served. The ticket does not shorten the wait; it may change nothing at all about how quickly the staff work. What it changes is the customer's sense of control. A person holding ticket 48 who sees that number 31 is being called can estimate the remaining time, decide whether to step outside for a coffee, and stop scanning the room anxiously. Knowing replaces guessing, and guessing, it turns out, is exhausting.

[4] Fairness matters too, sometimes more than speed. People will accept a long line with surprising patience if they believe everyone is being treated the same way, but they become angry quickly when someone cuts in or when the next line seems to move faster than theirs. For this reason, some supermarkets have replaced several short lines—one for each cashier—with a single long line that feeds all the cashiers in turn. On average, the single line does not move customers through the store any faster, and at first glance it may even look more discouraging. But it removes the painful experience of choosing the "wrong" line and watching strangers who arrived later reach a cashier first. The wait becomes, in the customer's eyes, a shared and just one.

[5] Finally, the end of a wait shapes the memory of the whole. People do not record experiences the way a camera does; they keep a few highlights, especially the most intense moment and the final one. A wait that ends with a warm greeting and quick service is often remembered more kindly than a shorter wait that ends with a rude clerk. Some amusement parks use this knowledge deliberately. They post estimated waiting times that are slightly longer than the real ones, so that visitors who reach the front "early" feel pleasantly surprised rather than cheated.

[6] Critics point out that these techniques can be used to avoid fixing real problems. A government office that installs a television in its waiting room might feel less pressure to hire the extra staff it actually needs. A company that manages how waiting feels may have little reason to reduce how long it lasts. In this view, the psychology of waiting is less a science of comfort than a science of distraction, and customers should be wary of it.

[7] Those who study lines tend to answer that both goals can be pursued at once. Shorter waits are always welcome, but no organization can remove waiting entirely, because demand rises and falls in ways that no schedule can perfectly predict. Given that some waiting is unavoidable, they argue, it makes sense to ask not only "How long?" but also "How does it feel?" The answer to the second question, unlike the answer to the first, can often be improved with a mirror, a ticket, or a single honest line.
questions.q: The main purpose of the passage is to:
c: argue that businesses should spend more money on staff so that customers never have to wait.
explain why the felt length of a wait can differ from its real length and describe how organizations respond to that difference.
describe the history of the numbered-ticket system used in clinics and government offices.
prove that single lines move customers through supermarkets faster than several short lines.
questions.e: B covers the whole passage: felt vs real time (paragraph 1), the principles (2–5), the criticism and reply (6–7). A goes beyond even the critics' point, C is one detail, and D is reversed: paragraph 4 says the single line is NOT faster on average.

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, the complaints about the elevators largely stopped because:
c: the engineers' upgrades made the elevators faster.
the manager explained to tenants why the elevators were slow.
fewer tenants used the elevators after the mirrors were installed.
the people waiting had something to look at.
questions.e: Paragraph 2 says the complaints stopped "not because the elevators moved any faster but because people now had something to look at." A is directly contradicted (the cheaper idea replaced the upgrades); B and C are never mentioned.

questions.q: The story about the office building (paragraph 2) mainly serves to:
c: illustrate the idea that occupied time feels shorter than unoccupied time.
show that engineers usually suggest solutions that are too expensive.
prove with exact measurements that mirrors reduce waiting time.
introduce the criticism that waiting techniques are only distractions.
questions.e: The paragraph states the principle ("empty time stretches") and ends by linking the story to it. B is too broad (one story, not "usually"); C is too extreme: the author even admits the story may not be true in every detail; D belongs to paragraph 6.

questions.q: Based on paragraph 3, the main benefit of a numbered-ticket system is that it:
c: makes the staff serve customers more quickly.
allows customers to leave the building without losing their place.
lets customers predict how much longer they will wait.
reduces the total number of customers who come to the office.
questions.e: The paragraph says the ticket changes "the customer's sense of control": the person can "estimate the remaining time." A is wrong because the ticket "may change nothing at all about how quickly the staff work." B is half-right: stepping outside is only one result of knowing the time, not the main benefit. D is never stated.

questions.q: As it is used in the last sentence of paragraph 4, the word just most nearly means:
c: only.
fair.
recent.
exact.
questions.e: The whole paragraph is about fairness: no one who arrived later reaches the cashier first, so the wait is "shared and just" = fair. "Only" and "exact" are common meanings of "just" but do not fit this sentence (the common-meaning trap). "Recent" has no support.

questions.q: According to the passage, how does a single line that feeds several cashiers compare with several separate lines?
c: It moves customers through no faster on average, but it feels fairer to the people waiting.
It moves customers through faster, and it looks shorter at first glance.
It moves customers through more slowly, so customers become angry more quickly.
It moves customers through at the same speed, but customers can no longer choose a cashier they like.
questions.e: Paragraph 4: the single line "does not move customers through the store any faster" and it removes the pain of picking the "wrong" line. B reverses both facts (it may look MORE discouraging). C contradicts the passage. D starts correctly (half-right) but the second half is never mentioned.

questions.q: According to paragraph 5, some amusement parks post waiting times that are longer than the real ones in order to:
c: discourage visitors from joining lines that are already crowded.
make the lines appear more popular than they are.
give staff extra time to prepare each ride.
make visitors feel pleasantly surprised when the wait ends sooner than expected.
questions.e: The paragraph says the longer estimates are posted "so that visitors who reach the front 'early' feel pleasantly surprised rather than cheated." The other reasons sound possible in real life, but the passage never gives them (outside-knowledge trap).

c: give further examples that support the principles described in paragraphs 2–5.
explain how television screens make waiting rooms more comfortable.
present an objection to the use of techniques that change how waiting feels.
show that government offices are worse at managing lines than private companies.
questions.e: The paragraph opens with "Critics point out" and warns that the techniques may be "a science of distraction." A is reversed (it questions the principles, it does not support them). B is a detail used for the opposite point. D compares two groups the paragraph never ranks.

questions.q: In the last paragraph, the people who study lines respond to the critics mainly by arguing that:
c: because some waiting cannot be avoided, improving how waiting feels is worthwhile alongside shortening it.
shorter waits are less important than pleasant waits.
organizations can remove waiting entirely if they plan their schedules carefully.
customers should be wary of any organization that installs mirrors or televisions.
questions.e: Paragraph 7: "both goals can be pursued at once" and "some waiting is unavoidable." B is too extreme (shorter waits "are always welcome"). C is directly contradicted ("no organization can remove waiting entirely"). D is the critics' view, not the answer to it.

blocks.title: Remember
items: 36 questions in 40 minutes = about 10 minutes per 9-question passage set; 27 questions (3 passages) are scored.
Read once, actively: blurb, first and last paragraphs, a 3-word label per paragraph, one-sentence main idea.
Answer reference questions first and big-picture questions last.
Every right answer is proved by a sentence in the passage; every wrong answer has a nameable trap.
No penalty for wrong answers: answer all 36.
